full_judgment:
2. is the suit bad for misjoinder and non joinder of parties? 

 4. As regard the first ground Mr. T. Ali, the learned advocate for the respondent frankly conceded and we think rightly that it was a case of non inclusion of a necessary party then the learned Subordinate Judge was clearly because in the absence of such persons the suit is not properly constituted and no effective decree can be passed by the Court. As to the second ground the proposition stated by learned Subordinate Judge is generally correct. Order 1, rule 13 or the Code of Civil Procedure provides as follows:- 

 "All objections on the ground of non-joinder or mis-joinder of married shall be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and in al cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement unless the ground of objection has subsequently arisen and any such ohiection not so taken shall be deemed to have been waived". 

 5. On the evidence adduced in the case we do not think that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in taking the view that there is no satisfactory evidence about possession of any non-empleaded parties. The contesting defendants have adduced some evidence to show that Fatu Bibi and one Ismail who are not parties to the suit are in possession of some portion of the disputed land. As regards Ismail, nothing has been mentioned in the written statement. In the evidence given by D W.4 who is an unsummoned witness, there is a statement to the effect that to the east of Rahim Bux's house and to the south of Abdul Razzak's house is the house of Ismail Shabed. It has not been definitely stated that Ismail's house stands on a portion of the disputed land D.W 5 alone says that Ismail's house is upon the disputed land. In view of the absence of any pleading in this respect, it difficult to hold reliving upon this piece of evidence that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in his assessment that Ismail was not a necessary the suit. But the Question of Fatu Bibi stands on a different footing. It has been clearly asserted in the written statement that Fakir Chand and his sister Fatu Bibi purchased a portion of C.S 383 from Defendant No. 15 on 30-11-54 and have built a residential house where they have been living with their families. The registered deed of sale by which Rahim Bux sold the said land to Fakir Chand and Fatu Bibi has been marked Ext B(1). Fakir Chand has been made Defendant in the suit on the allegation that Defendant Nos. 1-14 are in actual occupation alleging that they are tenants under Defendant Nos. 15-17. The case sought to be made out at the trial was that the Defendant was in possession but they were trespassers. So, we think it cannot be successfully assailed that Fakir Chand who claims on the basis of Ext. B(1) is in possession of a portion of the disputed land, as included in Ext B(1). In that view of the matter the possession of Fatu Bibi can hardly be disputed. In our view [Fatu Bibi was a necessary party to the suit but due to her absence, the entire suit can not fail. The plaintiffs can be non-suited only in respect of the land appertaining to C. S. plot No. 383 because it is only in this plot in which Fatu Bibi is interested and is in possession.]
